clue.text: Henry has one objection to fish

parts.note: Hal is the familiar short form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
the Roman numeral for one is I
a 'but' is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'

explanation.surface: Henry has a single complaint about the fish on his plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A large flatfish of northern seas, often eaten as steak.

clue.text: Silver in one's house is done by one's vassals.

indicators.note: in places the symbol for silver inside the word for one's house

parts.note: one's house is one's home
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Polishing the silver in the house is a job for the servants.
explanation.walkthrough: A vassal in feudal times publicly pledged allegiance to his lord; that ceremony is what is done.
explanation.definitionFit: Feudal vassals paid formal tribute of allegiance to their lord.

clue.text: .Teutonic siren

parts.note: a German river maiden of legend whose singing lured Rhine boatmen onto a rock

explanation.definitionFit: In German legend a maiden sings on a rock above the Rhine and lures sailors to their deaths.

clue.text: Brachycephalic vegetable:

parts.note: a short-skulled person is broad-headed, and 'bean' is slang for the head, so the vegetable is a broad-headed one

explanation.walkthrough: Brachycephalic means having a broad, short skull; 'bean' is old slang for the head, so a broad bean is a broad head.
explanation.definitionFit: A large flat pulse grown in kitchen gardens, also called the fava.

clue.text: Stupid in, an unusually osseous way

explanation.surface: Someone stupid in a strangely bony fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Osseous means bony: the second reading takes the answer literally, a head with too much bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull-witted people are said to have dense skulls; literally it describes an unusually bony cranium.

clue.text: Argued — with breath no longer restrained ?

explanation.surface: Someone argued passionately, no longer holding their breath.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as DE-BATED: 'bated' is the restrained breath of 'with bated breath', and the prefix DE- undoes it.
explanation.definitionFit: To discuss a motion formally is to argue it; the second reading undoes the 'bated' state of held breath.

clue.text: "With thee fade away into the forest *"(Keats)

definitions.text: "With thee fade away into the forest *"(Keats)

parts.words: "With thee fade away into the forest *"(Keats)
parts.note: the missing last word of a line from Keats's Ode to a Nightingale

explanation.surface: A quotation from Keats with its final word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Ode to a Nightingale reads 'And with thee fade away into the forest' followed by the missing adjective; the asterisk marks the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective Keats uses for the forest means shadowy or faintly lit.

clue.text: Scotland's slatternly sweeper

explanation.surface: A slovenly Scottish broom.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots the word is a contemptuous term for a slovenly woman; elsewhere it is a broom of twigs.
explanation.definitionFit: A twig broom sweeps; in Scottish speech the same word scorns an untidy woman.

clue.text: Job for a horse

parts.note: a horse whose work is a particular brisk two-beat gait, raced in harness

explanation.definitionFit: A horse bred and trained for harness racing at a particular gait.

clue.text: Knit two together, for instance, as being in order

indicators.note: being in places the word 'as' within the word for an order

parts.note: a decree is an official order

explanation.surface: Knitting instructions followed in sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knit two together' is a knitting instruction that loses a stitch, an example of reducing.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitting two stitches as one reduces the stitch count, which knitters call a reduction of this name.

clue.text: Doctor Right has singular philosophy of religion

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a standard crossword abbreviation for a doctor
monism is the philosophical doctrine that reality is a single substance

explanation.surface: A doctor named Right holds an unusual one-substance view of religion.
explanation.definitionFit: The faith of the Latter-day Saints, founded by Joseph Smith, is a religion.

clue.text: One last letter backed by the first one

definitions.text: One last letter backed by the first one

parts.words: One last letter backed by the first one
parts.note: describes a follower of a school whose first teacher was Zeno, a name starting with Z, the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A puzzle about alphabetical order, with one letter supported by another.
explanation.walkthrough: Zeno of Citium founded the school that taught in the Stoa, the painted porch in Athens; his name begins with the last letter, and he was the first of the school, so a member is one backed by him.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of Zeno's philosophical school, which taught calm acceptance, is one of his followers.

clue.text: Eels often sound so cold

indicators.note: the clue asks for the way the word for eels' usual preparation is pronounced

parts.note: eels are often served jellied, a London East End dish

explanation.surface: Eels often seem chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: Jellied eels, eels set in their own cold jelly, are a traditional London street food; the word said aloud is close to the Latin-derived word for icy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a literary term for icy or freezing.

clue.text: This stone has yet to come to Britain by the way

definitions.text: This stone has yet to come to Britain by the way

parts.words: This stone has yet to come to Britain by the way
parts.note: a roadside marker stone measuring distance in a metric unit, which British roads, still measured in miles, do not use

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain stone has not yet reached Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' means beside the road, not 'incidentally': British milestones count miles, so the metric equivalent has not arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: A metric distance of a thousand metres, which on continental roads replaces the mile on roadside stones.

clue.text: Old Portuguese U-boat victims of 1915?

explanation.surface: Elderly Portuguese sailors sunk by a submarine in the First World War.
explanation.walkthrough: Lusitania was the Roman province roughly covering Portugal; the Cunard liner Lusitania was sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the Roman province of Portugal, and those aboard the liner torpedoed in 1915.

clue.text: One — over — the — eightsome ? What a game !

definitions.text: One — over — the — eightsome ? What a game !

parts.words: One — over — the — eightsome ? What a game !
parts.note: one more than eight is nine, and an eightsome of men suggests a morris side; together they name an old board game

explanation.surface: Someone who has had one over the eight at a reel exclaims at the fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for slightly drunk, and an eightsome is a Scottish reel. Read literally, one plus eight men gives nine men in a morris side, naming an old board game played with nine pieces each.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient board game for two in which each player has nine counters to form rows of three.

clue.text: Study of snakes involves holy pig and two ducks

indicators.note: involves, in its sense of entangling or rolling up, signals the letters being twisted together

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, written as O, so two ducks are OO

explanation.surface: Snake study apparently needs a sacred pig and a pair of ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involves' rearranges HOLYPIG with OO, the two ducks.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of zoology concerned with serpents.

clue.text: How to meet posterity's growing need for newspaper material ?

definitions.text: How to meet posterity's growing need for newspaper material ?

parts.words: How to meet posterity's growing need for newspaper material ?
parts.note: planting trees on land now so that future generations have wood pulp for paper

explanation.surface: A question about supplying future readers with newsprint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growing' does double duty in the surface: the need increases, and trees grow to meet it.
explanation.definitionFit: To plant land with trees, which supply the pulp for newsprint.

clue.text: But no airy phantom from *the lowlands

definitions.text: But no airy phantom from *the lowlands

parts.words: But no airy phantom from *the lowlands
parts.note: a real airman from the Netherlands, the Low Countries, rather than the legendary ghost ship

explanation.surface: A denial that a ghost comes from low-lying country.
explanation.walkthrough: The legend is a phantom ship doomed to sail forever; the clue asks for the phrase read literally, a Dutch pilot, who is solid rather than airy.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the legendary ghost ship, read literally, describes a Dutch aviator.

clue.text: Gave in out or up

parts.note: one verb that means surrendered, produced and relinquished

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to give in (submit), give out (produce a crop) and give up (surrender).

clue.text: Draw vehicle overturned in a kind of race '

indicators.note: in places the turned vehicle inside the race

parts.note: TT, Tourist Trophy, is the motorcycle race held on the Isle of Man

indicators.note: overturned turns the word for the vehicle backwards

parts.note: a cart is a simple vehicle

explanation.surface: A cart tips over in a race and draws a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' turns CART into TRAC, which goes 'in' TT.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw in, as a magnet or a crowd does, is to pull towards.

clue.text: Like minstrels, except one in the Washington district

parts.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the abbreviation for the district

parts.note: DC, District of Columbia, is the federal district containing Washington
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Everyone in Washington's district except one is like a minstrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bards were poet-singers, so the adjective describes minstrels.

clue.text: Vernal ode composed by such a proverbial 'camel ?

indicators.note: composed suggests the letters being put together afresh, as a poem is composed

explanation.surface: A spring poem written about a famously burdened camel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges VERNAL ODE. The camel is the proverbial one whose back was broken by the last straw.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel in the proverb carries so heavy a load that one straw more breaks its back.

clue.text: On a legendary ship, many a musical movement

indicators.note: on in a down clue means placed above, so the numeral sits on top of the ship

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword way of saying many
the Argo carried Jason and the Argonauts in Greek legend

explanation.surface: Many crew aboard a legendary ship enjoy a slow piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow, broad movement in a musical work takes its name from the tempo marking.

clue.text: East German one has a port in old Italy

parts.note: Ost is the German word for east
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An East German man owns a harbour in ancient Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East German' is not a person from the former GDR but the German word for east.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient harbour city at the mouth of the Tiber served as Rome's port.

clue.text: Senior metal-joiner beheaded

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter is cut off the word for the metal-joiner

parts.note: a welder joins pieces of metal by fusing them

explanation.surface: A senior metalworker loses his head.
explanation.definitionFit: An older person, or a church official, is a senior.

clue.text: French artist putting the swing into London?

definitions.text: French artist putting the swing into London?

parts.words: French artist putting the swing into London?
parts.note: the painter of the Rococo picture The Swing, which hangs in London's Wallace Collection

explanation.surface: A French artist brings some swing to the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the swing' is the painting The Swing (1767), held by the Wallace Collection, a London gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A French Rococo painter whose most famous picture, The Swing, hangs in London.

clue.text: In which Venice one held the gorgeous East

definitions.text: In which Venice one held the gorgeous East

parts.words: In which Venice one held the gorgeous East
parts.note: echoes Wordsworth's sonnet on Venice: 'Once did she hold the gorgeous East in' followed by the missing word for feudal tenure

explanation.surface: A line about Venice ruling the splendid Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's 'On the Extinction of the Venetian Republic' opens 'Once did she hold the gorgeous East in fee'; 'one' here is the clue's 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold in fee is to hold as a feudal possession, so the word names that tenure.

clue.text: Fisher. J, with his pre-Tale tail

definitions.text: Fisher. J, with his pre-Tale tail

parts.words: Fisher. J, with his pre-Tale tail
parts.note: Mr Jeremy Fisher is Beatrix Potter's frog, who before his story began would have been a young frog with a tail

explanation.surface: A judge named Fisher had a tail before his tale was told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fisher J' looks like a judge (J is the title of a High Court judge), but it is Jeremy Fisher of Beatrix Potter's The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher; before the Tale he had a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A frog's larval stage, with a tail and gills, comes before the adult frog.

clue.text: Bloody discouraging

parts.note: read as discouraging blood, that is, stopping a bleed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like an intensifier for 'very discouraging', but it is the blood being discouraged from flowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance that stops bleeding by contracting blood vessels, as a shaving pencil does.
